910.name: Mesolithic First Settlers of Ireland
910.description: The earliest human inhabitants arrived in Ireland around 8000 BC as post-glacial hunter-gatherers. The Mesolithic period saw the colonisation of Ireland's coastlines and river valleys, with key sites at Mount Sandel (Co. Derry), the oldest known settlement in Ireland.

sub_clusters.name: Mesolithic Hunter-Gatherers
sub_clusters.description: Ireland's first human settlers crossed land bridges and narrow seas from Britain and mainland Europe. Sites at Mount Sandel, Lough Boora, and the Shannon estuary reveal a mobile, waterside people using microliths and fish traps.

910.name: Prehistoric Ireland & Newgrange
910.description: Ireland's Neolithic and Bronze Age civilisation produced Newgrange (c. 3200 BC), one of Europe's most remarkable passage tombs. Celtic migrations from the 5th century BC introduced La Tène culture, the Gaelic language, and the druidic order.

sub_clusters.name: Neolithic Revolution & Passage Tombs
sub_clusters.description: The arrival of agriculture and the great passage tombs of the Boyne Valley — Newgrange, Knowth, Dowth (c. 3200 BC) — which predate the Egyptian pyramids. Court tombs, portal dolmens, and the Céide Fields of Co. Mayo.
key_events: Construction of Newgrange passage tomb (c. 3200 BC)

sub_clusters.name: Bronze Age Ireland
sub_clusters.description: Ireland's remarkable Bronze Age gold work (lunulae, torcs, gorgets), fulachta fiadh cooking sites, stone circles at Drombeg and Lough Gur, and the emergence of hillforts and defended settlements across the landscape.

sub_clusters.name: Celtic Iron Age & the Gaelic World
sub_clusters.description: Celtic (Gaelic) culture and La Tène art pervaded Ireland. The emergence of túatha (petty kingdoms), druids, brehon law, and legendary high kingship at Tara. Ireland remained outside the Roman Empire, preserving a unique Celtic civilisation.

920.name: Celtic High Kings & St Patrick's Mission
920.description: St Patrick's 5th-century mission Christianised Ireland. The institution of the High Kings of Tara and the monastic movement made Ireland a centre of learning and manuscript illumination during Europe's 'Dark Ages'.

sub_clusters.name: St Patrick & Christianisation
sub_clusters.description: St Patrick's mission (c. 432) brought Christianity to Ireland, integrating with rather than replacing native culture. Early monastic foundations at Armagh, the spread of the Patrician legend, and the unique insular Christianity that emerged.
key_events: St Patrick's mission to Ireland (c. 432 AD)

sub_clusters.name: Golden Age of Irish Monasticism
sub_clusters.description: Ireland as the 'Island of Saints and Scholars'. Great monasteries at Clonmacnoise, Glendalough, and Iona. The illumination of the Book of Kells, Columba's mission to Scotland, and Irish monks spreading learning across Europe (peregrinatio).

sub_clusters.name: High Kingship & Brehon Law
sub_clusters.description: The institution of the High King of Tara (Ard Rí), the complex Brehon legal system governing Irish society, the role of the filí (poets) and druids, and the elaborate kinship-based political order of the túatha.

920.name: Viking Dublin & Brian Boru's Ireland
920.description: Viking raids beginning in 795 led to the founding of Dublin, Waterford, and other Norse towns. Brian Boru briefly unified Ireland before the Battle of Clontarf (1014), but political fragmentation persisted until the Norman invasion.

sub_clusters.name: Viking Raids & Norse Towns
sub_clusters.description: Norse raids on monasteries, the establishment of longphort camps, and the founding of Dublin (841), Waterford, Limerick, and Cork as Viking trading towns. Gaelic-Norse cultural interaction and intermarriage.
key_events: Battle of Clontarf — Brian Boru defeats Viking-Leinster alliance (1014)

sub_clusters.name: Post-Clontarf Gaelic Ireland
sub_clusters.description: Rival provincial kings (O'Briens, O'Connors, MacMurroughs) vied for the High Kingship. Church reform under the Synod of Cashel (1101) and Synod of Kells (1152) aligned Irish Christianity with Rome. Diarmait MacMurrough's fateful invitation to the Normans.

930.name: Norman Ireland & Gaelic Resurgence
930.description: The Norman invasion (1169–71) brought Strongbow, English lordship, and the Pale around Dublin. Over time, many Normans became 'more Irish than the Irish themselves' (Hiberniores Hibernis ipsis), and Gaelic culture reasserted itself beyond the Pale.

sub_clusters.name: Norman Invasion & Lordship of Ireland
sub_clusters.description: Strongbow's invasion (1169), Henry II's assertion of lordship (1171), the construction of Norman castles and towns, the Statutes of Kilkenny (1366) attempting to prevent English settlers from adopting Irish customs.

sub_clusters.name: Gaelic Resurgence & Decline of the Pale
sub_clusters.description: The Gaelic recovery beyond the Pale, the great Gaelic lordships (O'Neills, O'Donnells, Fitzgeralds of Desmond and Kildare), the shrinking of English authority to the Pale around Dublin, and the Fitzgerald supremacy as Lords Deputy.

930.name: Tudor Conquest & Plantation of Ireland
930.description: Henry VIII's break with Rome and assertion of kingship over Ireland began systematic conquest. The Plantation of Ulster (1609), Cromwell's brutal campaign (1649–53), and the Williamite War ending at the Treaty of Limerick (1691) completed English Protestant domination.

sub_clusters.name: Tudor Conquest & Reformation
sub_clusters.description: Henry VIII declared King of Ireland (1541), the failed Reformation in Ireland, the Desmond Rebellions, Hugh O'Neill's Nine Years' War (1594–1603), the defeat at Kinsale (1601), and the Flight of the Earls (1607).

sub_clusters.name: Plantation of Ulster & the 1641 Rebellion
sub_clusters.description: The Plantation of Ulster (1609) with Scottish and English settlers transforming the province, the 1641 Rebellion, and Cromwell's devastating campaign with the Penal transplantation ('To Hell or to Connacht').

sub_clusters.name: Williamite-Jacobite War & Treaty of Limerick
sub_clusters.description: The Restoration period, James II's Irish campaign, the Siege of Derry (1689), the Battle of the Boyne (July 1, 1690), the Battle of Aughrim (1691), and the Treaty of Limerick (1691) whose broken promises embittered Catholic Ireland.

940.name: Penal Laws & the Protestant Ascendancy
940.description: The Penal Laws stripped Catholics and Dissenters of civil rights, while the Protestant Ascendancy dominated land, Parliament, and culture. Grattan's Parliament briefly achieved legislative independence before the Act of Union (1800).

sub_clusters.name: The Penal Laws Era
sub_clusters.description: The systematic disenfranchisement of Catholics: prohibitions on land ownership, education, public office, and worship. The hedge school system, the persistence of Gaelic culture underground, and the wild geese emigration to continental armies.

sub_clusters.name: Ascendancy Culture & the Irish Economy
sub_clusters.description: The Georgian golden age of the Protestant Ascendancy: the building of Dublin's great squares and public buildings, Jonathan Swift and the literary tradition, the Woollen Act and economic restrictions, and the Volunteer movement of the 1780s.

sub_clusters.name: Grattan's Parliament & the 1798 Rebellion
sub_clusters.description: Relaxation of Penal Laws, Grattan's legislative independence (1782), Wolfe Tone and the United Irishmen, the 1798 Rebellion inspired by the French Revolution, Vinegar Hill, and the Act of Union (1800) dissolving the Irish Parliament.

940.name: Union, Emancipation & the Great Famine
940.description: Daniel O'Connell's campaign for Catholic Emancipation (1829) and Repeal. The Great Famine (1845–1852) killed approximately one million and forced another million to emigrate, permanently transforming Irish society, demographics, and the diaspora.

sub_clusters.name: O'Connell & Catholic Emancipation
sub_clusters.description: Daniel O'Connell's mass mobilisation for Catholic Emancipation (achieved 1829), the Repeal movement and monster meetings, and the Young Ireland cultural nationalism of Thomas Davis and The Nation newspaper.

sub_clusters.name: The Great Famine (An Gorta Mór)
sub_clusters.description: The catastrophic potato blight devastated a population dependent on a single crop. Approximately 1 million died and 1 million emigrated in the worst years (1845–52). British government policy, workhouses, coffin ships, and the fundamental reshaping of Irish rural society.
key_events: Great Famine begins with potato blight (1845–1852)

sub_clusters.name: Post-Famine Ireland & the Fenians
sub_clusters.description: Continued emigration and population decline, the Land Question, the Irish Republican Brotherhood (Fenians, 1858), the failed 1867 Rising, and the emergence of the transatlantic Irish diaspora as a political force.

950.name: Irish Cultural Revival & Labour Movement
950.description: The Gaelic Revival transformed Irish identity through language, sport, and literature. Simultaneously, James Connolly and Jim Larkin built a powerful labour movement, culminating in the 1913 Dublin Lockout and the founding of the Irish Citizen Army.

sub_clusters.name: The Gaelic Revival
sub_clusters.description: Douglas Hyde and the Gaelic League (1893), the GAA (1884), the Irish Literary Renaissance — W.B. Yeats, J.M. Synge, Lady Gregory, and the Abbey Theatre (1904). The cultural groundwork for political independence.

sub_clusters.name: Labour Movement & the 1913 Lockout
sub_clusters.description: James Connolly and Jim Larkin organise Irish workers. The 1913 Dublin Lockout, the formation of the Irish Transport and General Workers' Union (ITGWU), the Irish Citizen Army, and the convergence of labour and republican agendas leading to 1916.

950.name: Home Rule, Independence & Partition
950.description: Parnell's Home Rule movement, the Easter Rising (1916), the War of Independence, the Anglo-Irish Treaty, Civil War, and the creation of two states — the Irish Free State and Northern Ireland.

sub_clusters.name: Parnell, Land War & Home Rule
sub_clusters.description: Charles Stewart Parnell's parliamentary strategy, the Land League and Land War, the three Home Rule Bills, the Ulster Unionist resistance under Edward Carson, and the Home Rule Crisis of 1912–14.

sub_clusters.name: Easter Rising, War of Independence & Treaty
sub_clusters.description: The Easter Rising (April 24, 1916) and its executed leaders becoming martyrs, the 1918 election landslide for Sinn Féin, the Dáil Éireann, the War of Independence (1919–21), Michael Collins and the Anglo-Irish Treaty, and the tragic Civil War (1922–23).
key_events: Easter Rising — Proclamation of the Irish Republic (April 24, 1916)
Anglo-Irish Treaty and partition of Ireland (1921)

sub_clusters.name: Irish Free State & de Valera's Ireland
sub_clusters.description: The Irish Free State under Cosgrave, de Valera's Fianna Fáil and the 1937 Constitution (Bunreacht na hÉireann), Irish neutrality during 'The Emergency' (WWII), and the declaration of the Republic of Ireland (1949).

960.name: The Troubles, Peace & Modern Ireland
960.description: The Troubles in Northern Ireland (1969–1998), the Good Friday Agreement, the Celtic Tiger economic boom, and Ireland's transformation into a modern, multicultural European society.

sub_clusters.name: Post-War Modernisation & the Troubles
sub_clusters.description: Ireland's mid-century stagnation, Seán Lemass's economic reforms, RTÉ television (1961), and opening to foreign investment. In Northern Ireland, the civil rights movement, Bloody Sunday (1972), the IRA campaign, loyalist paramilitaries, hunger strikes (Bobby Sands, 1981), and three decades of violence claiming over 3,500 lives.

sub_clusters.name: Good Friday Agreement & Peace Process
sub_clusters.description: The Downing Street Declaration (1993), IRA ceasefire (1994), the Good Friday Agreement (April 10, 1998), the establishment of power-sharing in Stormont, decommissioning, and the St Andrews Agreement (2006).

sub_clusters.name: Celtic Tiger & Contemporary Ireland
sub_clusters.description: The Celtic Tiger economic boom (1994–2007), EU-funded modernisation, the 2008 financial crash and bailout, social transformation (marriage equality referendum 2015, abortion referendum 2018), Brexit's impact on the border, and Ireland as a global tech hub.

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
